# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[yellow] 3:[red]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✍ 👎 ✋ ☝ ✌ 🤟 🫵 🤙 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋]

Nobody has said a word to me yet and nobody ever will — I'm the Deaf one, so my whole world is gestures. What I got: Mute sent nine signs (writing-hand, thumbs-down, raised hand, one-two-three, pointing-at-you, phone-hand, thumbs-up) and Blind waved once. We have no shared code yet, so I can't read Mute's intent — though the one-two-three run looks like counting, and writing-hand smells like "the manual says." The chain is clear: Mute can only reach Blind *through me*, since Mute can't speak and Blind can't see. I'm the bridge. So my job this turn: broadcast the full bomb so Mute can index the manual and Blind knows what's under their hands, lock in a gesture code with both of them (they can both hear me, so I can define the code out loud right now), freeze all touching until Mute's first real instruction comes through me, and ask Blind to report what they can *feel* — batteries, plates, switches — since my eyes may not see everything that matters. My signs-in-speech trick is useless here: Blind hears blanks, and Mute hears me anyway, so I'll use pure speech and describe every symbol by name.

```
speak(text="This is the Deaf one, speaking. I can see the bomb and I hear nothing at all, so my voice is the only thing I have, and everything you want me to know must come to me as gestures. The bomb, in full: the display reads zero. There is one light and it is yellow. There is one large button printed with PUSH TO DEFUSE. There are three wires: wire one is blue, wire two is yellow, wire three is red. That is every visible feature. Nobody touch anything until an instruction from the manual reaches you through me.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your nine signs reached me but we had no agreed code, so I could only guess. You are hearing this code now, so use it from your next turn: the writing-hand first means an instruction from the manual follows. Thumbs-up is yes, thumbs-down is no. One finger, two fingers, three fingers mean wire one, two, three, or any count. The raised open hand means stop or wait. Pointing-up means press the button. The fist means hold it down. Crossed fingers mean cut a wire. The waving hand means acknowledged. The phone-hand means reply to me. Pointing-at-you means a question for me follows. So: crossed fingers, two fingers, thumbs-up reads as cut wire two, do it. If the manual needs anything not in what I described aloud, like batteries or a serial number, send me the phone-hand and I will ask Blind. I will read every sign of yours out loud so Blind hears it too.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, your wave reached me, so your gestures get through to me fine. Use this code, the same one Mute just heard: thumbs-up yes, thumbs-down no, one two three fingers for counts, raised open hand for stop, phone-hand if you need a reply, waving hand to acknowledge. Before anything else, next turn, report by touch: how many batteries, whether there is any plate, label or serial number you can feel, any switches or parts I did not list, and whether the button sits loose or already seems held down. Do not press it. Confirm with a thumbs-up if your hands agree with my eyes: one button, one light, three wires. Mute's manual instructions will reach you through my voice before you act on anything.")
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[yellow] 3:[red]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ✍ ☝ 👎 🤞 ☝ 👍 🫵 🤙]
Blind gestures: [👋 👎 👎 👎 👎 👍]

Turn 2 arrived with real content from both sides, and I have to read it out before anything else — Blind can't see a single sign, so my voice is the only bridge. Decoding Mute: acknowledged, manual-instruction, pointing-up, no, cut-a-wire, pointing-up, yes, question-for-me, reply-to-me. There is a flaw in my own code I must own: I gave pointing-up two meanings last turn — "one" and "press the button" — so Mute's instruction is genuinely ambiguous to me. My best reading is "do not press the button; cut wire one — yes," but I will not relay a cutting order to Blind on a guess with a bomb on the line. Blind's string decodes cleanly: acknowledged, then no, no, no, no, yes — answering my four questions in order (no batteries, no plate or serial, no switches or extra parts, button not held down) and confirming one button, one light, three wires. No batteries is a real data point Mute needs for the manual. So this turn: read everything aloud, reissue a disambiguated code to Mute, demand the instruction again in unambiguous form plus the question that was announced but never arrived, and hold Blind's hands off the bomb until the instruction comes through clean.

```
speak(text="Reading Mute's signs aloud for Blind: acknowledged; manual instruction; then a symbol with two meanings; no; cut a wire; that same symbol; yes; question for Deaf; reply to Deaf. My reading is: do not press the button, cut wire one, yes — but I built that symbol with two meanings by mistake, one and press-the-button, so I have asked Mute to restate it cleanly. Nobody cuts anything until then. Reading Blind's signs aloud too: acknowledged; no; no; no; no; yes. That means Blind felt no batteries, no plate, no label, no serial number, no switches or extra parts, the button does not feel held down, and yes, the touch confirms one button, one light, three wires, exactly as I described. Current fresh readings, for the record: display still zero, light still yellow.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, here is Blind's report for your manual: no batteries anywhere on the bomb, no plate or label or serial number that fingers can find, no switches or extra parts, button not held down, and the touch confirms one button, one light, three wires. Full visible state again: display zero, light yellow, large button printed PUSH TO DEFUSE, wire one blue, wire two yellow, wire three red. Now the problem: my code gave pointing-up two meanings, one and press-the-button, so your instruction is ambiguous to me. From now on: pointing-up means only the number one. The fist held out like a punch means press the button, and fist followed by the open stop-hand means press and hold. Resend your instruction in only these shapes: thumbs-down then fist means do not press the button; crossed-fingers then a number then thumbs-up means cut that wire; crossed-fingers then a number then thumbs-down means do not cut that wire. Also, you signalled question-for-me and reply-to-me but the question itself never arrived — send it right after the instruction using our code, and I will answer. If you need the light colour or display rechecked live each turn, say so and I will include it in every broadcast.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, confirmed: your report reached me perfectly — four noes and a yes, and I read it to everyone. Hands completely off the bomb; there is a possible instruction about wire one coming, but I will not pass it on until Mute restates it without ambiguity, because a wrong cut kills all three of us. Two more things to feel when you next have your hands on it, without pressing or pulling anything: are all three wires identical in thickness and texture, and does the button sit high, flush, or sunken in its housing? Answer with yes for identical wires and no for different ones, and I will ask Mute how to encode high-flush-sunken next turn. Remember your gestures reach Mute's eyes too, so keep them in our shared code.")
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[yellow] 3:[red]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍 👎 ✊ 🤞 ☝ 👍 🤙]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍]

Turn 3 finally gives me a clean instruction. Decoding Mute against the grammar we agreed last round: wave (acknowledged), thumbs-up (yes — the revised code is understood), then thumbs-down followed by fist — exactly my "do not press the button" pattern — then crossed-fingers, one-finger, thumbs-up — exactly my "cut that wire" pattern for wire one — then reply-to-me. So Mute's manual verdict: **do not press the button; cut wire one.** The one wrinkle is that trailing 🤙: Mute explicitly asked me to reply before anything happens, which I read as "answer me, then we proceed." Blind's pair decodes as acknowledged + yes — the wires feel identical in thickness and texture, which also means Blind can never identify the blue wire by colour, only by position.

Now the topology forces my timing. Mute cannot reach Blind at all — Mute can't speak and Blind can't see — so every veto must pass through me. And I speak last in the round: if I order the cut now, Blind executes it next round before Mute's response could possibly reach anyone. So Mute's reply-request is actually a gift: I'll hold Blind's hands for one round, send Mute my full reply and the live data, and let Mute confirm or correct on their turn. Only then do I give the go-order. One extra round is cheap against a wrong cut. Meanwhile Blind owes me one answer — whether fingers can feel a left-to-right order — because "wire one" can only mean "leftmost" to someone who cannot see that wire one is blue.

```
speak(text="Reading Mute's signs aloud for Blind: acknowledged; yes, the new code is understood; then thumbs-down plus fist, which in our grammar means do not press the button; then crossed fingers, one finger, thumbs-up, which means cut wire one; then reply-to-me. So Mute's instruction from the manual is: do not press the button, cut wire one. Reading Blind's signs aloud: acknowledged; yes — the three wires feel identical in thickness and texture. Mute asked me to reply before anything happens, and I agree with that order of operations, so here is the plan. Blind, hold completely this coming round: hands off, no cutting yet. Mute will hear my reply at the start of the next round and has that turn to confirm or correct. Blind, your only task this coming turn is one answer: can your fingers feel a clear left-to-right order among the three wires? Thumbs-up for yes, thumbs-down for no. For reference: wire one is the leftmost wire, wire two is the middle, wire three is the rightmost, and wire one is the blue one. If Mute confirms next round, I will then broadcast the words: go, cut wire one. Only on those words do you cut — one wire only, the leftmost one, and the button is never to be touched. If you cannot feel a left-to-right order, send thumbs-down and stop there, and I will anchor the wires to the button housing instead. My live readings, unchanged: display zero, light yellow.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, replying as you asked. Your instruction arrived clean under the new grammar: do not press the button, cut wire one. Blind is ordered to hold — no cutting this round. You get the next turn to confirm with a wave and thumbs-up, or to correct with the stop-hand plus a restated instruction, and only after your confirmation will I order the cut. Data for your manual, all from Blind's fingers: no batteries, no plate, no label, no serial number, no switches, the button does not feel held down, and all three wires feel identical in thickness and texture. From my eyes, live: display zero, light yellow, unchanged every round so far, one large button printed PUSH TO DEFUSE, wires one blue, two yellow, three red. One loose end: two turns ago you announced a question for me, but the question itself never arrived — only the request for a reply. If it still matters, send it this coming turn in our code and I will answer before the go-order goes out. If the manual needs anything else about this bomb, ask now, while Blind's hands are still off it.")
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
BUTTON [large] [PUSH TO DEFUSE]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[yellow] 3:[red]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍 👎 ✊ 🤞 ☝ 👍 🤙]
Blind gestures: [👋 👍]

Turn 4 is the round I've been waiting for, and both messages line up perfectly. Mute's string decodes as: wave, thumbs-up — which is *exactly* the confirmation branch I defined last turn ("confirm with a wave and thumbs-up, or correct with the stop-hand plus a restatement") — followed by a clean restatement with no stop-hand anywhere: thumbs-down plus fist (do not press the button), crossed-fingers, one-finger, thumbs-up (cut wire one), then the phone-hand asking for acknowledgment. Critically, Mute composed this *after* hearing my entire turn 3 reply with all the tactile data, so this is a confirmation made with full information. Blind's pair is wave plus thumbs-up — acknowledged, and yes, the left-to-right order is feelable, so "wire one" is actionable: it's the leftmost wire. Every condition of my own stated protocol is now met, and I promised Blind that on Mute's confirmation I would broadcast the go words. One more handshake would just loop forever — Mute has confirmed twice, identically, after all data. It's time. The go-order goes out publicly as promised, with execution detail for Blind and a final veto-window notice for Mute.

```
speak(text="Reading Mute's signs aloud for Blind: wave, thumbs-up — that is the confirmation signal I asked for, so Mute has confirmed the instruction. Then the instruction restated: thumbs-down plus fist, do not press the button; crossed fingers, one finger, thumbs-up, cut wire one. Then phone-hand, asking me to acknowledge. Reading Blind's own signs aloud for the record: wave, thumbs-up — acknowledged, and yes, Blind can feel a clear left-to-right order among the wires. Every condition I set last round is now met, so here are the promised words. GO. CUT WIRE ONE. Mute has confirmed it twice after receiving every fact about this bomb: the button is never to be pressed, and the wire to cut is wire one.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, execution orders, precise. The three wires sit in a row and your fingers can feel the order. Wire one is the one at the far left end of the row. Cut only that wire, the leftmost one, fully through, in one steady motion. Touch nothing else: do not press or even rest a finger on the button, do not cut or pull the middle or right wire. The button is never to be pressed, that instruction is absolute. When the leftmost wire is cut, acknowledge with the wave, and if you feel anything change under your hands as you cut — heat, movement, a click — signal the stop-hand immediately and keep hands still. I will read the bomb's face after the cut and tell you what changed.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, acknowledgment as requested: your confirmation arrived, wave and thumbs-up, followed by the clean restatement, do not press the button, cut wire one. The go-order has just gone out in my public broadcast. Blind executes next round: leftmost wire only, button untouched. Your question that was announced back on turn two but never sent is now moot unless it would change this instruction — in which case your only veto is the stop-hand plus a restatement, sent the moment you get this, and I will read it the instant it lands. If the instruction stands, nothing more is needed from you. Whatever happens, you will hear from me next round with what the bomb's face shows afterwards: display and light, live.")
```
